title: Glivenko-Cantelli Theorem (Uniform Law of Large Numbers)
description: The Glivenko-Cantelli theorem is the uniform law of large numbers: for i.i.d. real-valued random variables X₁, X₂, ... with CDF F(x) = P(X₁ ≤ x), the empirical CDF Fₙ(x) = (1/n)|{i ≤ n : Xᵢ ≤ x}| converges uniformly to F almost surely. This strengthens the pointwise SLLN to simultaneous convergence over all thresholds x ∈ ℝ.

meta.author: Glivenko (1933), Cantelli (1933)
meta.assumptions: 3 axioms: thresholdIndicator_integrable (bounded measurable function integrability), integral_thresholdIndicator_eq_cdf (E[1_{X≤x}] = F(x)), glivenko_cantelli_uniform (finite bracketing argument for uniform convergence — not in Mathlib 4.26). Pointwise convergence theorem is fully proved via SLLN.

mathlibDependencies.description: Strong Law of Large Numbers for real-valued i.i.d. functions: pairwise-independent identically-distributed integrable functions have sample means converging a.s. to their expectation.
Composition of i.i.d. functions with a measurable function remains i.i.d.
Composition of identically-distributed functions with a measurable function remains identically distributed.

overview.historicalContext:
The Glivenko-Cantelli theorem was proved independently by Soviet mathematician Valery Glivenko and Italian actuary Francesco Cantelli in back-to-back papers in the same 1933 volume of the Giornale dell'Istituto Italiano degli Attuari. Cantelli had earlier (1917) proved the first almost-sure convergence result for the SLLN, and this 1933 result was the natural sequel: not just pointwise but uniform convergence. The theorem is often called the 'fundamental theorem of statistics' because it validates nonparametric inference from first principles — the empirical CDF, without any assumption about the true distribution, converges to the true CDF uniformly and surely.

The same year (1933), Kolmogorov proved that $\sqrt{n} \cdot \sup_x |F_n(x) - F(x)|$ has a limiting distribution (the Kolmogorov distribution), giving quantitative rates beyond what Glivenko-Cantelli provides. This is the theoretical basis of the Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) test: reject $H_0: F = F_0$ when $D_n = \sup_x |F_n(x) - F_0(x)|$ exceeds the critical value from Kolmogorov's distribution. The statistic $D_n$ is literally the uniform norm studied in this file.

Donsker (1952) proved the functional CLT: the process $\sqrt{n}(F_n - F)$, viewed as a random element of $C[0,1]$, converges weakly to a Brownian bridge $B(F(\cdot))$. This is the deep stochastic-process generalization that subsumes both Glivenko-Cantelli ($D_n \to 0$) and Kolmogorov's limit theorem (limiting distribution of $\sqrt{n} D_n$).

Vapnik and Chervonenkis (1971) generalized Glivenko-Cantelli from indicator classes indexed by half-lines to arbitrary measurable sets $A$ in a VC class $\mathcal{C}$: $\sup_{A \in \mathcal{C}} |P_n(A) - P(A)| \to 0$ a.s. The key quantity is the VC dimension, which measures the 'complexity' of $\mathcal{C}$. This is the mathematical foundation of PAC learning (Valiant 1984) and the VC bound on generalization error in statistical learning theory. Talagrand's work (1994–1996) on concentration inequalities further sharpened these results via the transportation inequality and generic chaining.
overview.problemStatement: Let $X_1, X_2, \ldots$ be i.i.d. real-valued random variables with CDF $F(x) = P(X_1 \leq x)$. Define the empirical CDF $F_n(x) = \frac{1}{n}|\{i \leq n : X_i \leq x\}|$. Then $$\sup_{x \in \mathbb{R}} |F_n(x) - F(x)| \xrightarrow{a.s.} 0 \quad \text{as } n \to \infty.$$
overview.text: The empirical CDF converges uniformly to the true CDF almost surely for any i.i.d. sequence.
overview.proofStrategy: The formalization proceeds in two stages. Stage 1 (proved): For each fixed threshold x, the indicators 1_{Xᵢ ≤ x} are i.i.d. Bernoulli(F(x)) random variables. Applying Mathlib's `strong_law_ae_real` gives Fₙ(x) → F(x) a.s. for each x. Stage 2 (axiomatized): For ε > 0, choose finitely many continuity points q₁,...,qₖ of F partitioning ℝ with F-mass < ε per interval. Pointwise convergence holds simultaneously on the finite grid a.s. (finite intersection). For any x between grid points, monotonicity gives |Fₙ(x) - F(x)| ≤ max_j |Fₙ(qⱼ) - F(qⱼ)| + ε, establishing uniform convergence. The bracketing argument is axiomatized as `glivenko_cantelli_uniform` since the finite covering infrastructure is not available in Mathlib 4.26.
keyInsights: The key insight is that uniform convergence follows from pointwise convergence plus monotonicity of both Fₙ and F, via a finite bracketing argument
Indicator functions 1_{Xᵢ ≤ x} transform the problem into SLLN for Bernoulli random variables, connecting to Mathlib's existing `strong_law_ae_real`
The `iIndepFun.comp` lemma is crucial: i.i.d. real random variables composed with the threshold indicator remain i.i.d.
The uniform convergence step requires continuity points of F (every CDF has uncountably many) and is the main gap with Mathlib 4.26
Glivenko-Cantelli is the simplest case of empirical process theory; the Vapnik-Chervonenkis generalization extends this to arbitrary VC classes

The Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic $D_n = \sup_x |F_n(x) - F(x)|$ is exactly the uniform norm studied here; its a.s. convergence to 0 (Glivenko-Cantelli) and its $\sqrt{n}$-rescaled limiting distribution (Kolmogorov 1933) are the two central facts of nonparametric goodness-of-fit testing

sections.title: Imports, Namespace, and Variable Declarations
sections.summary: Opens the GlivenkoCantelli namespace, imports Mathlib.Probability.StrongLaw, Independence.Basic, and IdentDistrib, and declares abstract variables: any measurable space Ω, measure μ.
sections.mathContext: The abstract setup Ω : Type*, [MeasurableSpace Ω], μ : Measure Ω ensures the theorem applies to any probability space, not only ℝ-valued sample spaces.

sections.title: Empirical and True CDF Definitions
sections.summary: Defines empiricalCDF as the sample mean of threshold indicators, trueCDF as μ{ω | X₀(ω) ≤ x}.toReal, and thresholdIndicator as the composition of X_i with the Iic indicator function.
sections.mathContext: empiricalCDF X n x ω = (1/n) * Σᵢ 1_{Xᵢ(ω) ≤ x}; trueCDF X μ x = (μ{ω | X₀(ω) ≤ x}).toReal

sections.title: Basic Algebraic Identities
sections.summary: Proves empiricalCDF_eq_mean (empirical CDF is a ratio of summed indicators, proved by ring) and thresholdIndicator_eq_comp (indicator equals a function composition), enabling iIndepFun.comp and IdentDistrib.comp.
sections.mathContext: F_n(x,ω) = (Σᵢ 1_{Xᵢ≤x}(ω)) / n; Y_i(x,ω) = (1_{·≤x}) ∘ X_i makes composition lemmas applicable.

sections.title: Measurability of Indicator Functions
sections.summary: Proves measurability of v ↦ 1_{v ≤ x} as a real-valued Borel function, using measurable_const.indicator measurableSet_Iic.
sections.mathContext: The composition structure thresholdIndicator X x i = (1_{· ≤ x}) ∘ X i is key for applying iIndepFun.comp.

sections.title: I.I.D. Structure of Threshold Indicators
sections.summary: Proves identical distribution via IdentDistrib.comp, and pairwise independence via iIndepFun.comp + iIndepFun.indepFun. These are the two key hypotheses for SLLN.
sections.mathContext: If X_i ~ X₀ (IdentDistrib) and X_i are iIndepFun, then 1_{Xᵢ ≤ x} ~ 1_{X₀ ≤ x} and are pairwise independent.

sections.title: Integration Axioms: Integrability and E[1_{X₀≤x}] = F(x)
sections.summary: Axiomatizes thresholdIndicator_integrable (bounded measurable functions on probability spaces are integrable) and integral_thresholdIndicator_eq_cdf (the expected value of the threshold indicator equals the true CDF). Both are provable in principle but require careful Mathlib API navigation.
sections.mathContext: ∫ 1_{X₀≤x} dμ = μ{ω | X₀(ω) ≤ x} = F(x). Uses integral_indicator_const and measurability of {X₀ ≤ x}.

sections.title: Pointwise Convergence via SLLN
sections.summary: PROVED: For each fixed x, Fₙ(x) → F(x) a.s. Applies strong_law_ae_real to threshold indicators, then uses integral_thresholdIndicator_eq_cdf to identify the limit as trueCDF.
sections.mathContext: strong_law_ae_real gives (Σᵢ 1_{Xᵢ ≤ x})/n → E[1_{X₀ ≤ x}] = F(x) a.s. Requires pairwise independence and identical distribution.

sections.title: Uniform Convergence (Glivenko-Cantelli)
sections.summary: AXIOM: sup_x |Fₙ(x) - F(x)| → 0 a.s. The bracketing argument for uniform convergence is axiomatized as glivenko_cantelli_uniform since finite covering infrastructure is absent from Mathlib 4.26.
sections.mathContext: The bracketing uses: (1) continuity points of F are dense; (2) finite grid gives simultaneous a.s. convergence; (3) monotonicity of Fₙ and F control off-grid error.

sections.title: Structural Properties: Monotonicity, Non-Negativity, Error Vanishing
sections.summary: Proves that both the empirical and true CDFs are monotone non-decreasing (via indicator monotonicity and measure monotonicity) and non-negative. Also derives that the pointwise error Fₙ(x) - F(x) → 0 a.s. as a corollary of pointwise convergence.
sections.mathContext: Monotonicity: Iic x ⊆ Iic y for x ≤ y gives 1_{·≤x} ≤ 1_{·≤y} pointwise, so F_n(x) ≤ F_n(y). Non-negativity follows from positivity of indicators and measures.

conclusion.summary: This formalization captures the Glivenko-Cantelli theorem with 3 axioms. The pointwise convergence theorem is fully proved from Mathlib's SLLN via the i.i.d. structure of threshold indicators. The uniform convergence step is axiomatized, as the finite bracketing argument requires continuity-point infrastructure not yet in Mathlib 4.26.
conclusion.implications:
**Statistical Foundations**: The KS statistic $D_n = \sup_x |F_n(x) - F_0(x)|$ is exactly the uniform norm in this formalization. Glivenko-Cantelli ($D_n \to 0$ a.s.) provides consistency; Kolmogorov's limit theorem ($\sqrt{n} D_n \to$ Kolmogorov distribution) provides the null distribution for hypothesis testing. The KS test is one of the most widely used nonparametric tests in science: it requires no parametric assumption about $F_0$ and rejects when $D_n$ is large.

**Empirical Process Theory**: Glivenko-Cantelli is the zeroth-order result in empirical process theory. The first-order result is Donsker's theorem (1952): the process $\mathbb{G}_n = \sqrt{n}(F_n - F)$, as a random function of $x$, converges weakly in $\ell^\infty(\mathbb{R})$ to a Gaussian process $B(F(x))$ (a Brownian bridge). Donsker's theorem gives the asymptotic distributions of all statistics of the form $T(F_n)$, including the KS statistic, the Cramér-von Mises statistic, and the Anderson-Darling statistic.

**Statistical Learning Theory**: The VC generalization (Vapnik-Chervonenkis 1971) replaces the half-line class $\{(-\infty, x] : x \in \mathbb{R}\}$ with any VC class $\mathcal{C}$ of sets. The VC dimension $d$ of $\mathcal{C}$ controls the rate: $\mathbb{E}[\sup_{A \in \mathcal{C}} |P_n(A) - P(A)|] \le C\sqrt{d/n}$. Setting $\mathcal{C}$ to be the half-spaces $\{x : \langle w, x \rangle > b\}$ (VC dimension = dimension + 1), the VC bound controls the generalization error of support vector machines and linear classifiers. This is the fundamental inequality underpinning PAC learning.

**Lean Formalization Design**: The `iIndepFun.comp` + `IdentDistrib.comp` pattern demonstrated here — transferring structural properties through measurable function composition — is a reusable blueprint for any application of SLLN to transformed random variables (e.g., moment estimates, $U$-statistics, empirical risk minimization).
openQuestions: Can the bracketing argument for glivenko_cantelli_uniform be formalized in Lean 4 using Mathlib's existing topology and measure theory infrastructure?
Can the Donsker CLT (weak convergence of √n(Fₙ - F) to a Brownian bridge) be formalized, giving quantitative rates for Glivenko-Cantelli?
What is the minimal Mathlib infrastructure needed for VC-class Glivenko-Cantelli generalizations?
